name: avatar
title: Avatar
description: A person or entity's image, falling back to initials when there is none.

props.name: name
props.description: The person or entity's name: both the fallback initials and the accessible name.
props.summary: The person or entity's name. Required — it is both the fallback initials and the accessible name.
use: Always. The name is what makes the fallback possible and the image describable.
dont: Passing an email or a user id. Initials derived from `a.hartley@` are not initials, and the accessible name would be an address.
props.a11y: Used as the image's `alt` when `decorative` is not set. When the image is missing, the initials are shown but the full name is still what is announced — a screen reader should never hear 'AH'.

props.name: src
props.description: Image URL. Omit, or let it fail, to fall back to initials.
props.summary: Image URL. Omit, or let it fail, to fall back to initials.
use: A real photo or logo. The fallback is automatic, so there is no need to branch on whether one exists.

props.name: size
props.description: Diameter, from the control scale so an avatar lines up with the controls beside it.
props.summary: Diameter, from the `size.control.*` scale so an avatar lines up with the controls beside it.
dont: Mixing sizes within one stack of avatars — they read as a set.

props.name: decorative
props.description: Marks the avatar as redundant to a name already on screen.
props.summary: Marks the avatar as redundant to a name already on screen.
use: An avatar immediately beside the person's name in a row — announcing it again is noise.
dont: Anything standing alone. Without adjacent text the avatar is the only thing identifying the person, so hiding it removes that identification entirely.
props.a11y: Renders `aria-hidden` with an empty `alt`. The `name` is still required, because it still produces the initials.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the avatar's wrapper.
use: Placing the component in its surrounding layout — a span, a width, a margin the parent cannot express.
dont: Overriding the size — the three steps are the scale, and a fourth written in a component's CSS is the drift the scale exists to prevent.
Restyling the component's internals through descendant selectors. Those are the approved token mapping, and overriding them here puts a second answer somewhere the contract cannot see.

usage.case: A photo with its name beside it
usage.when: A row in a member list, where the name is already text.
usage.example: Ada Hartley
usage.notes: `decorative` because the name is right there — announcing it twice is noise. Note `name` is still required: it is what produces the initials if the photo fails to load.

usage.when: An avatar in a toolbar or a stack, with no adjacent name.
usage.example: <Avatar name="Ada Hartley" src={user.photo} />
usage.notes: Not decorative: the avatar is the only thing identifying this person, so it carries the name.

usage.when: A user who has not uploaded a photo — which is most of them.
usage.example: <Avatar name="Ada Hartley" />
usage.notes: Initials are shown and the full name is announced. There is nothing to branch on: omitting `src`, and an `src` that 404s, land in the same place.

base.summary: A circular image, falling back to initials on the most recessed surface.

tokens.size: size.control.md, with the sm and lg steps at the other sizes — an avatar lines up with the controls beside it, which is the whole reason it borrows the control scale
tokens.edge: border.default solid theme.border.strong — the circle needs its own boundary or the fallback disappears against any container using theme.bg.muted, which is the tone the fallback itself takes. theme.border.default is not an option: composited over a mid surface it measures around 1.2:1
tokens.fallback background: theme.bg.muted — the most recessed surface, so initials read as a placeholder rather than a filled badge
tokens.fallback color: theme.fg.secondary — the pairing the muted background documents for text; theme.fg.muted falls to AA-large there
tokens.image fit: cover, so a non-square photo is cropped rather than squashed — a layout fact, not a token

name: badge
title: Badge
description: A small inline label for a status, a count, or a category.

props.name: children
props.description: The badge's text.
props.summary: The badge's text.
dont: A sentence. A badge that wraps is a Notice wearing the wrong component.

props.name: variant
props.description: Which role's tone the badge wears.
props.summary: Which role's tone the badge wears.
use: `neutral` for a count or a category — the default, and right whenever the badge is not reporting health.
`success` / `warning` / `danger` only for actual status, where the colour is telling the reader something the text also says.
dont: Colour as decoration. Five badges in five colours that mean nothing teaches readers to ignore the colour on the one that does.
`danger` for 'important'. It means something is wrong.
props.a11y: Every variant uses its role's subtle background with that role's foreground — never the saturated `bg`, which is a non-text indicator tone. The text carries the meaning; colour only reinforces it, so a badge is never colour-only.

props.name: dot
props.description: Renders a status dot before the text.
props.summary: Renders a status dot before the text.
use: A status badge in a dense table, where the dot is findable at a glance and the text confirms it.
dont: A dot with no text. A bare coloured dot is colour-only information, which is exactly what the variant contract forbids.
props.a11y: Decorative and `aria-hidden` — it repeats what the text already says.

usage.when: The commonest case: a number qualifying something next to it.
usage.example:
<Button>
  Messages
  <Badge>3</Badge>
</Button>
usage.notes: Neutral by default: a count is not a status, and colouring it would imply something about the number.

usage.case: A status in a table row
usage.when: Reporting health, where the colour reinforces text that already says it.
usage.example: <Badge variant="danger" dot>Failed</Badge>
usage.notes: The dot is decorative and aria-hidden. Removing it would lose nothing for a screen reader, which is the test of whether a visual flourish is safe.

usage.when: The text is a sentence explaining something.
usage.example: <Badge variant="warning">Your trial ends in three days, renew to keep your data</Badge>
usage.notes: Don't. That is a Notice: it has room for the sentence, a heading, and somewhere to put the action. A badge that wraps onto two lines has already stopped being a badge.

name: breadcrumbs
title: Breadcrumbs
description: The trail from the site's root to the current page.

props.name: items
props.description: The trail in order, root first. The last item is the current page.
props.summary: The trail in order, root first. The last item is the current page and is not a link.
use: Every ancestor of the current page, ending with the page itself.
dont: Omitting the current page. The trail ends at where you are; ending it at the parent leaves the reader unsure whether the last crumb is a link they are already on.
A trail that is not a hierarchy. Breadcrumbs say where this page sits, not how the user got here — history is the back button's job.
Giving the last item an `href`. It is the page you are on, and this component drops it.
props.a11y: Rendered as an ordered list inside a `<nav>`, so the count and the order are announced. The last item gets `aria-current="page"` and renders as text rather than a link.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
use: Changing it only when a page has more than one navigation landmark and they need telling apart.
props.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`. A page with several landmarks needs distinct names or they are indistinguishable in a landmark list.

props.name: separator
props.description: What sits between crumbs.
props.summary: What sits between crumbs.
dont: A character that carries meaning, such as an arrow implying a flow. The separator is punctuation.
props.a11y: Decorative and `aria-hidden`: the list structure already conveys the order, and announcing 'slash' between every crumb is noise.

usage.when: The ordinary case.
usage.example:
<Breadcrumbs
  items={[
    { label: "Home", href: "/" },
    { label: "Reports", href: "/reports" },
    { label: "Q3 revenue" },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: The last item has no `href` — it is the page you are on. It renders as text with `aria-current="page"` rather than a link to itself.

usage.when: A page that also has a primary nav and a pagination nav.
usage.example: <Breadcrumbs label="Breadcrumb" items={trail} />
usage.notes: Distinct `aria-label`s are what make landmarks tellable apart in a screen reader's landmark list. Two navs both called 'Navigation' are worse than one.

base.summary: A trail of links ending in the current page.

tokens.font-size: type.supporting.size — a trail is orientation, not content, so it sits below body size
tokens.link color: theme.accent-role.fg — the token documented for an inline link
tokens.current page color: theme.fg.primary — the end of the trail is where you are, so it reads as text rather than as another link
tokens.separator color: theme.fg.muted — punctuation, quieter than either crumb

name: button
title: Button
description: Primary, secondary, tertiary, and destructive actions in three sizes, with loading and icon-only modes.

props.name: variant
props.summary: Which action tier this button occupies, and therefore how loud it is.
use: `primary` for the single highest-priority action in a view — one per view.
`secondary` for a supporting action shown beside a primary one.
`tertiary` for low-emphasis actions in dense areas, like a row action.
`destructive` for an action that deletes or revokes something.
dont: Two `primary` buttons in one view — the tier is a claim about priority, and two claims cancel out.
`destructive` for merely irreversible actions like Submit; it means data is lost.
props.a11y: Variant is visual only. A destructive action still needs its own confirmation step — colour is not a warning.

props.name: size
props.summary: Control height and inline padding, from the `size.control.*` scale. Text size does not change with it.
use: `md` everywhere by default.
`sm` inside dense rows, toolbars, and table cells.
`lg` for a single prominent call to action on a marketing or empty-state surface.
dont: Shrinking to `sm` to fit a cramped layout — fix the layout budget instead.

Expecting the label to grow with it. All three sizes set the same text size, so `size` buys a bigger target for the same action rather than a louder one — and an icon inside, being sized from that text, does not change either.
Setting height or padding yourself; the size prop is the only supported way to change either.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks activation while keeping the button focusable and announced.
use: An action that is unavailable for a reason the surrounding UI already explains.
dont: Hiding why an action is unavailable — pair it with visible helper text or a tooltip.
Form validation gating, where an inline error explains more than a dead button does.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled`, never the native `disabled` attribute: the control stays in the tab order and discoverable by screen readers, and activation is blocked in the primitive's click guard.

props.name: loading
props.description: Shows a spinner and blocks activation while preserving focus.
props.summary: Shows a spinner and refuses activation while an operation is in flight.
use: Async work started by this button, so the same control reports its own progress.
dont: Page-level or unrelated loading — that belongs to the region that is actually loading.
Swapping the label to 'Loading…' as well; the spinner and `aria-busy` already say it, and a changing label loses the action's name.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-busy` alongside `aria-disabled`, so assistive technology hears both that the control is working and that it will not respond yet.

props.name: iconOnly
props.description: Square icon-only button; pass the icon as children and set aria-label.
props.summary: Square button carrying an icon and no visible text.
use: Dense toolbars and row actions where the icon is unambiguous and repeated.
Icon-only buttons in this system: there is no separate `IconButton` component, and one would be a second way to do what this prop already does.
dont: Any action whose icon is not already conventional — an unlabelled novel icon is unreadable.
Passing text children as well; the square sizing assumes a single glyph.
props.a11y: You MUST pass `aria-label`. Nothing in the component supplies an accessible name when there is no visible text.

usage.when: The most common pairing: one primary button that owns its own progress.
usage.example: <Button loading={saving} onClick={save}>Save changes</Button>
usage.notes: `loading` blocks repeat activation on its own — don't also guard with `disabled`.

usage.when: Deleting something, with the safe action given equal visual weight beside it.
usage.example: <Button variant="destructive" onClick={remove}>Delete project</Button>

usage.when: A dense table row where a labelled button would not fit.
usage.example: <Button variant="tertiary" size="sm" iconOnly aria-label="Remove row">×</Button>
usage.notes: Without `aria-label` this button has no accessible name at all.

behavior.summary: Activation guarding and disabled/busy semantics, independent of React and of any styling.

decisions.decision: `aria-disabled` instead of the native `disabled` attribute
decisions.why: A natively disabled button leaves the tab order and stops being announced, so users navigating by keyboard or screen reader cannot discover that the action exists. Activation is blocked in the click guard instead.

decisions.decision: `loading` implies inert
decisions.why: One flag covers both halves of what callers actually want — show progress, and refuse a second click — so the two cannot be set inconsistently.

primary.summary: The single highest-priority action in a view.

tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, so `size` changes the box and not the label
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — do not swap the background

secondary.summary: A supporting action shown next to a primary one. Its label is accent-toned rather than neutral, so the outlined button still reads as an action and not as a disabled box — the border alone carries very little at this fill.

tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes

destructive.summary: An action that deletes or revokes something.

tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes

name: button-group
title: Button Group
description: A named set of related buttons, spaced or attached into one bar, horizontal or vertical.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the group. Required unless `labelledBy` names an existing element.
props.summary: Accessible name for the group — what these buttons have in common.
use: Always, unless `labelledBy` points at a visible heading that already says it.
Naming the group by its subject rather than its shape: "Row actions", not "Button group".
dont: Restating the buttons' own labels — "Save and Cancel" tells a screen reader what it is about to read anyway.
Leaving it off because the group looks obvious on screen; an unnamed group adds a level to navigate and says nothing about what is inside it.
props.a11y: Becomes the group's `aria-label`. Every group MUST have a name from this or from `labelledBy` — the component cannot supply one, because only the caller knows what the buttons have in common.

props.name: labelledBy
props.description: Id of an element that already names this group — a heading above it, typically.
props.summary: Id of an element that already names this group, used instead of a written label.
use: A visible heading sits directly above the group and says the same thing a label would.
dont: Pointing at an element that is conditionally rendered — a dangling `aria-labelledby` leaves the group unnamed with no visible sign of it.
props.a11y: Wins over `label` when both are passed, because it points at text the user can see: when the visible heading changes, the name changes with it.

props.name: orientation
props.summary: Which way the buttons stack.
use: `vertical` in a narrow rail or a menu-like column where a row would wrap.
dont: `vertical` as a substitute for a menu — a list of navigation choices is a menu, not a stack of buttons.
Switching orientation per breakpoint by swapping the prop mid-interaction; pick one per layout and let the group wrap if it must.
props.a11y: Presentational only. It sets a data attribute for styling and deliberately does not set `aria-orientation`, which would promise arrow-key navigation this group does not implement.

props.name: attached
props.description: Joins the buttons into one continuous bar, with only the outer corners rounded.
props.summary: Joins the buttons into one continuous bar, with shared borders and only the outer corners rounded.
use: Actions that are variations of one thing and are read as a unit — a pager's Previous/Next, a split of one action into its two directions.
dont: Actions of different weight. Attaching a primary to a destructive makes them look like one control with two halves, which is exactly the moment a mis-click costs the most.
Expressing a choice. Attached buttons that hold a selected state are a `toggle-button-group`, and it says so to assistive technology; this one does not.
props.a11y: Visual only — nothing about the attached form changes what is announced. The buttons stay separately focusable either way.

usage.case: Two actions at the end of a form
usage.when: The default case: a primary action and its escape hatch, spaced rather than joined.
usage.example:
<ButtonGroup label="Form actions">
  <Button variant="secondary">Cancel</Button>
  <Button>Save changes</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
usage.notes: Spaced, not attached — these are two different decisions, and joining them makes them read as one control.

usage.when: Two halves of the same action, which is what `attached` is for.
usage.example:
<ButtonGroup label="Pagination" attached>
  <Button variant="secondary" iconOnly aria-label="Previous page">‹</Button>
  <Button variant="secondary" iconOnly aria-label="Next page">›</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
usage.notes: `iconOnly` still requires its own `aria-label` on each button — the group's name says what the pair is, not what each half does.

usage.case: Named by a heading that is already on screen
usage.when: The group sits under a heading that says exactly what the label would have said.
usage.example: Export
usage.notes: Prefer this to a written `label` whenever the heading exists: one string, visible, and it cannot drift from what the group actually contains.

usage.when: A narrow column where a horizontal row would wrap into an unreadable grid.
usage.example:
<ButtonGroup label="Layer actions" orientation="vertical">
  <Button variant="tertiary">Bring forward</Button>
  <Button variant="tertiary">Send backward</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
usage.notes: Still tab-navigated, not arrow-navigated. If the column is long enough that tabbing through it is tedious, it wants to be a menu.

behavior.summary: The group's accessible name and its grouping role — the two things the buttons inside cannot own between them. No selection state and no value: a button group runs actions, it does not hold an answer.

decisions.decision: `role="group"` with a required accessible name, not `role="toolbar"`
decisions.why: A toolbar is a single tab stop with arrow-key navigation between its controls. That is right for a dense, persistent bar of many actions and wrong for the common case here — two or three buttons in a card footer — where collapsing them into one tab stop makes them harder to reach, not easier. Groups that genuinely want toolbar semantics should say so explicitly rather than getting them by accident from a layout wrapper.

decisions.decision: Each button keeps its own tab stop
decisions.why: Follows from the role decision above. It also keeps the group composable: a `Button` inside a group behaves exactly like a `Button` outside one, so nothing about focus or activation has to be re-learned.

decisions.decision: Orientation is a data attribute, not `aria-orientation`
decisions.why: Orientation here changes how the group stacks and nothing else. `aria-orientation` announces a navigation direction, which would promise arrow-key movement this group deliberately does not implement.

decisions.decision: No per-item position data — corner joining is `:first-child`/`:last-child` in CSS
decisions.why: The DOM already knows which button is first and last. Emitting `data-position` would be a second copy of that fact, and a copy that goes stale the moment a button is conditionally rendered.

decisions.decision: Not a selection control
decisions.why: A group whose items hold a pressed state is `toggle-button-group`: it needs a value, a selection mode, and roving focus, none of which belong in a container for plain actions. Keeping them separate is what stops this component growing a `value` prop that only makes sense half the time.

spaced.summary: The default: buttons that belong together but read as separate controls.

tokens.item border-radius: radius.element — each button keeps the corners it sets for itself

attached.summary: Buttons joined into one continuous bar.

tokens.outer corner border-radius: radius.element, as logical corners so the bar flips in RTL
tokens.collapsed shared border: negative margin of border.1, so adjacent borders read as one
tokens.focused item stacking: raised above its neighbours so the focus ring is not clipped — a stacking fix, not a token

name: checkbox
title: Checkbox
description: A single on/off choice, with an indeterminate state for a parent summarising its children.

props.name: label
props.description: The checkbox's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
props.summary: The checkbox's label. Always required — `labelHidden` can take it off screen, but nothing removes it.
use: Always. A checkbox with no label is a control nobody can describe.
dont: Using the surrounding sentence as the label and leaving this empty — the binding is what makes the text a hit target and an accessible name.
Passing an empty string. An empty label is an unnamed control; hide it with `labelHidden` instead.
props.a11y: Rendered as a real `<label for>` bound to the input, so clicking the text toggles the box. Still a real label when hidden — only its pixels go away.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A checkbox in a table row or header cell, where the column already names what is being toggled and repeating it per row would be noise.
A dense control panel where the box sits directly under a heading that names it.
dont: Hiding it to save space in a form. In a form the label is the last thing to cut; if space is short the layout budget is wrong.
Hiding it on a standalone checkbox. With no adjacent text naming it, the label is the only thing saying what agreeing to this means.
Hiding it and then relying on a neighbouring cell's position to explain the box — position is not a name, and it is the first thing lost when a layout reflows.
props.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound by `for`, so the accessible name is unchanged — it is clipped, not removed. Not `display: none`, which would take the name with it. The required marker goes off screen with it; `aria-required` still carries that.

props.name: checked
props.description: Whether the box is checked. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the box is checked. Makes the component controlled.
use: Whenever the value lives outside the component, which is most of the time.
dont: Passing it without `onCheckedChange`; the box would render its state and then refuse to change it.
props.a11y: Drives the native checked state, which is what assistive technology reports.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled checkbox. Conflicts with `checked`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled checkbox.
use: Genuinely local state nothing else reads.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.description: Called with the state the box should move to, not the one it is leaving.
props.summary: Called with the state the box should move to, not the one it is leaving.
dont: Reading `event.target.checked` instead of the argument — they agree, but the argument is the one this component promises.

props.name: indeterminate
props.description: A parent summarising children that disagree. Outranks `checked`.
props.summary: Shows the box as neither checked nor unchecked: a parent summarising children that disagree.
use: A 'select all' box above a list where only some rows are selected.
dont: Expressing 'unknown' or 'not yet answered'. It means partially checked, and a screen reader announces it as `mixed`.
Combining it with a `checked` that is also true and expecting both to show — indeterminate wins visually and in what is announced, which is why they are not one prop.
props.a11y: Announced as `aria-checked="mixed"`. Set as a DOM property by this component, because HTML has no such attribute.

props.name: description
props.description: Helper text under the label.
props.summary: Helper text under the label.
dont: Error text. A checkbox that is invalid belongs in a field wrapper that owns the message.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
use: Linking an external label, or a scroll-to-error that needs the id to survive a re-render.
dont: Reusing one id across two checkboxes — the derived description id would collide too.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks activation while keeping the box focusable and announced.
props.summary: Blocks activation while keeping the box focusable and announced.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled` and refuses activation. Never the native `disabled` attribute, which would remove it from the tab order.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the checkbox as required.
props.summary: Marks the checkbox as required to assistive technology and in the label.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-required`. The visible marker is the label's job.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the checkbox's wrapper.
use: Placing the component in its surrounding layout — a span, a width, a margin the parent cannot express.
dont: Restyling the box. Its size, border and fill are the approved mapping.
Restyling the component's internals through descendant selectors. Those are the approved token mapping, and overriding them here puts a second answer somewhere the contract cannot see.

usage.when: The commonest case: one box, one label, its own state.
usage.example:
<Checkbox
  label="Email me product updates"
  checked={subscribed}
  onCheckedChange={setSubscribed}
/>

usage.when: Some rows selected, so the parent is neither checked nor unchecked.
usage.example:
<Checkbox
  label="Select all"
  checked={all}
  indeterminate={some && !all}
  onCheckedChange={toggleAll}
/>
usage.notes: `indeterminate` is what a screen reader hears as `mixed`. It is deliberately separate from `checked`, because it answers a different question: not this box's value, but whether the children below agree.

usage.when: A choice that cannot be made yet, whose current state still matters.
usage.example: <Checkbox label="Ship to billing address" checked disabled />
usage.notes: aria-disabled and a refused activation, never the native `disabled` attribute — the box stays focusable so a keyboard user can find it and read its state.

usage.case: A column of boxes under a heading that names them
usage.when: A table or a settings grid where the column header already says what is being toggled.
usage.example: <Checkbox label="Notify by email" labelHidden checked={row.email} onCheckedChange={…} />
usage.notes: `labelHidden` hides the pixels, not the name: the `<label for>` is still rendered and still bound, so each box is announced as "Notify by email" exactly as it would be with the label visible. The hit target shrinks to the box itself, which is the cost of this choice — it is why the visible label is the default.

behavior.summary: Checked state, the indeterminate third appearance, and the activation guard. Built on a native input[type=checkbox] so keyboard, form participation and the checked semantics come from the platform rather than being re-implemented.

decisions.decision: A native input, not a div with role="checkbox"
decisions.why: Space to toggle, participation in a form's data, and the checked state itself are all free from the platform and all easy to get subtly wrong by hand. The visual is drawn by a sibling element; the input stays in the DOM and keeps the semantics.

decisions.decision: `indeterminate` is a separate prop, not a third value of `checked`
decisions.why: It answers a different question. `checked` is this control's own value; `indeterminate` says the control is standing in for a set of children that disagree. A tri-state `checked` would force every caller to handle a value that only a parent checkbox can ever have, and would make the common two-state case read as incomplete.

decisions.decision: Indeterminate is set as a DOM property, never an attribute
decisions.why: There is no `indeterminate` content attribute in HTML — only an IDL property — so it cannot be expressed in JSX and has to be assigned to the element. The wrapper owns that, which is the whole reason this component cannot be a bare styled input.

decisions.decision: Activation is guarded, not disabled
decisions.why: This system's disabled controls stay focusable and announced. `readOnly` is the input analogue used by text-field, but it has no effect on a checkbox, so the guard here is a refused activation plus aria-disabled — the same shape as the button primitive.

decisions.decision: The label is required and is a real `<label for>`
decisions.why: A checkbox's hit target should include its text, and a bound label gives that for free. It also means the accessible name cannot drift from what is on screen.

base.summary: A single on/off choice, with a third appearance for a parent summarising its children.

tokens.box size: size.icon.md — the box is sized to the glyph it holds, so it takes the icon scale rather than the control one; the control heights are row heights and would dwarf the box itself
tokens.row height: no reserved row height. An earlier version set it to size.control.md for a bigger hit target, but with the box aligned to the first line that reserved 12px of dead space under every row and inflated the list's pitch to 40px. At the resulting 28px pitch the target conforms through WCAG 2.5.8's spacing exception: 24px circles centred on adjacent targets do not intersect. The label is bound, so the target is the full width of the text as well
tokens.control height: one line tall, from calc(type.control.size.md x type.control.line-height.md) = 20px. The line-height token is a unitless ratio, so it is not a length on its own — used alone the browser drops the declaration
tokens.border: border.default solid theme.border.strong — the same boundary tone text-field uses, tone-walked to the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control's edge
tokens.gap between box and label: space.gap.sm — the inline role, because this pairing is horizontal
tokens.gap between label and description: none — the label and the description each carry line-height leading, which already reads as 7px of separation. A gap on top of that made 11px and read as two unrelated lines
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — never a hand-written hover rule
tokens.outline (focus-visible): focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset — the offset is kept here, unlike text-field: a 20px box has no room for a flush ring to read as separate from its own border
tokens.border-radius: radius.inner — a nested square, which is what radius.inner names
tokens.checked mark: theme.fg.on-accent — the only foreground permitted on that fill, and it inverts with the accent in the dark scheme
tokens.indeterminate mark: theme.fg.on-accent on theme.accent-role.bg, drawn as a bar rather than a tick. The fill matches checked because the state is 'partly checked', not a third colour

example: <Checkbox label="Ship to billing address" checked disabled />

name: dialog
title: Dialog
description: Modal dialog with focus trapping, scroll locking, and dismiss behavior.

props.name: title
props.summary: The dialog's name. Required.
use: A noun phrase naming what this is about: “Delete project”, not “Are you sure?”
dont: A question. The title is the name, and “Are you sure?” names nothing — put the question in the body.
Leaving it out. It is required, and the type will not let you.
props.a11y: Rendered as an `<h2>` and wired with `aria-labelledby`, so the dialog announces with this name when it opens. A real heading, because a modal is its own outline — everything behind it is inert.

props.name: children
props.description: The dialog's content.
props.summary: The dialog's content.
use: What the reader needs in order to answer the title. It scrolls on its own if it is tall.
dont: Another dialog. Two modals deep, the reader has lost track of what the first one asked.
props.a11y: Scrolls in its own region so the title stays put and the footer actions stay reachable — a dialog taller than the viewport otherwise puts its buttons off-screen.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the dialog is showing. Always controlled — `showModal()` has no prop.
props.summary: Whether the dialog is showing. Always controlled.
use: Always. There is no uncontrolled mode, because `showModal()` is a method rather than an attribute and the component has to drive it.
dont: Expecting the dialog to close itself. Every dismissal arrives through `onClose`; setting this to false is what actually closes it.
props.a11y: Drives `showModal()` and `close()`. Nothing else makes the dialog modal — see the behaviour note.

props.name: onClose
props.description: Called when the dialog asks to close. Set `open` to false in it.
props.summary: Called when the dialog asks to close, with why.
use: Setting `open` to false.
Branching on the reason: `escape`, `close-button` or `backdrop` — a form might confirm on a backdrop click but not on the close button.
dont: Ignoring it. Nothing closes the dialog on its own, so an empty handler makes a dialog nobody can leave.
props.a11y: Focus returns to whatever opened the dialog automatically, because the platform restores it — you do not need to do it yourself.

props.name: description
props.description: A line under the title, wired as the dialog's description.
props.summary: A line under the title, wired as the dialog's description.
use: A consequence worth hearing with the name: “Everything in it goes too.”
dont: The whole body. It is announced along with the title, so a paragraph here is read before the reader has asked for it.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-describedby`. Omitted, there is no dangling reference — a describedby pointing at nothing is silently dropped by some screen readers and read as empty by others.

props.name: footer
props.description: The actions. Reads after the body it acts on.
props.summary: The actions.
use: One or two buttons, the primary one last.
The only way out when `dismissible` is false.
dont: Putting the close control here. That is what `dismissible` renders, placed and named for you.
props.a11y: Rendered after the body in DOM order, so the actions are reached after the content they act on.

props.name: size
props.summary: How wide it is allowed to get.
use: `sm` for a confirm — one question and two buttons.
`md` for a short form. The default.
`lg` for content that genuinely needs the room, such as a table.
dont: `lg` for a confirmation. A wide dialog with one sentence in it reads as a mistake, and the buttons end up a long way from the text.
props.a11y: Width only. Every size shrinks to fit a narrow viewport rather than overflowing it.

props.name: dismissible
props.summary: Whether the reader can close it themselves.
use: `true` — the default — for everything except the case below.
`false` for a blocking error where dismissing would lose work, or a decision that genuinely must be made now.
dont: A dialog with no footer action. Escape and the close button are the reader's escape hatches; removing both without giving them another traps them, which is the one thing this prop can do wrong.
`false` to stop people skipping something. A dialog that cannot be dismissed is a dialog people close by leaving the page.
props.a11y: `false` removes the close button and prevents the `cancel` event, so Escape does nothing. The footer then MUST contain a labelled way out.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the close button.
props.summary: Accessible name for the close button.
use: Translating it, or naming what is being closed when the context needs it.
dont: An empty string. The button is icon-only, so this is the only name it has.
props.a11y: Becomes the button's `aria-label`. Without it the control announces as an unnamed button, a 4.1.2 failure.

props.name: role
props.summary: ARIA's kind of dialog.
use: `alertdialog` when the dialog's whole content is a message needing a response — a destructive confirmation, a blocking error.
`dialog`, the default, for anything with work in it: a form, a panel, a picker.
dont: `alertdialog` for a form. It is announced more insistently and its description is read with its name, which is wrong for something the reader has to fill in and right for something they have to answer.
Reaching for it to make a dialog feel important. The role describes what the dialog is, not how much it matters.
props.a11y: A native `<dialog>` is already `role="dialog"`; this only ever narrows it to `alertdialog`, which the element cannot be on its own. Under `alertdialog` a screen reader reads `description` along with `title` rather than waiting to be asked, which is why the destructive confirmation below sets both.

props.name: initialFocus
props.summary: What to focus when it opens. Defaults to the platform's choice.
use: A destructive confirm, pointed at Cancel — so the dangerous button is not one Enter away.
A form, pointed at the first field.
dont: React's `autoFocus` instead. It does not work here: React calls `.focus()` during commit rather than emitting the attribute, so `showModal()` runs afterwards and applies its own default, undoing it.
props.a11y: Applied after `showModal()`, which is the only order that works. Left out, focus lands on the first focusable thing inside — usually the close button.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the dialog, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Rarely. `size` is the intended way to change its shape.
dont: Overriding the backdrop or the position. Both come from `dialog.css`, and a competing rule is how a modal ends up unreachable on one page.

usage.when: The commonest modal: one question, two ways out, and the dangerous one must not be the easy one.
usage.notes: `initialFocus` on Cancel is the point: without it focus lands on the first focusable thing, and a reader who opens this and presses Enter should not have deleted anything. `sm` keeps the buttons near the sentence. `alertdialog` is the role for this: the dialog's whole content is a question the reader has to answer, so the description is read along with the name instead of waiting to be asked.

usage.case: A blocking error, where dismissing would lose work
usage.when: Rare, and the only kind of dialog that should refuse to close.
usage.example:
<Dialog
  open={disconnected}
  onClose={() => {}}
  dismissible={false}
  title="Connection lost"
  footer={<Button onClick={reconnect}>Reconnect</Button>}
>
  Your changes are saved locally and will sync when you reconnect.
</Dialog>
usage.notes: The footer action is not optional here — with no close button and Escape blocked, it is the only way out, and a dialog like this without one traps the reader.

usage.case: Don't: a dialog opened from inside a dialog
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.example:
{/* Don't: by the time the second one is open, the reader has lost
    track of what the first one asked. */}
<Dialog open={editing} onClose={close} title="Edit project">
  <Button onClick={() => setConfirming(true)}>Delete project</Button>
  <Dialog open={confirming} onClose={closeConfirm} title="Delete project">
    This cannot be undone.
  </Dialog>
</Dialog>
usage.notes: Don't. Close the first, then ask — or ask inline in the dialog already open. The scroll lock and the focus trap both cope with stacking, so nothing breaks; it is the reader who loses the thread.

behavior.summary: A native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`. The browser supplies a real focus trap, `inert` on everything behind it, the top layer, `::backdrop`, Escape-to-close and focus returned to whatever opened it. A hand-written focus trap is the most bug-prone component in any design system, and the platform's is correct by construction — including for the cases hand-rolled ones miss, such as a screen reader's own navigation and the browser's find-in-page.

decisions.decision: `showModal()`, never the `open` attribute
decisions.why: Rendering `<dialog open>` shows the dialog NON-modally: no focus trap, no backdrop, and a live page behind it. There is no attribute for the modal state, only the method, which is why `open` is applied in an effect. Getting this wrong is the easiest way to ship a "modal" that is not one, and it looks correct on screen.

decisions.decision: `title` is required rather than optional
decisions.why: A modal with no accessible name is announced as "dialog" and nothing else. There is no sensible default and no case where omitting it is right, so the type refuses it instead of the contract asking nicely.

decisions.decision: The title is a real `<h2>`, unlike Notice's
decisions.why: A modal is genuinely its own context — everything behind it is inert — so the outline inside it starts fresh and the title is the top of it. A notice sits inside the page's existing outline and cannot know what level it is at, which is why that one is a styled paragraph.

decisions.decision: Escape is always prevented, then reported
decisions.why: The platform would close the dialog itself, leaving `open` still saying it is showing. Preventing the default and reporting through `onClose` keeps React the single source of truth for whether it is open.

decisions.decision: Initial focus is a ref, because React's `autoFocus` cannot work here
decisions.why: React implements `autoFocus` by calling `.focus()` during commit rather than by emitting the HTML attribute, so `showModal()` — which runs afterwards, in an effect — never sees an `[autofocus]` element and applies its own default, undoing it. `initialFocus` is applied after `showModal()` and therefore wins.

decisions.decision: The scroll lock counts holders rather than saving and restoring
decisions.why: Save-and-restore is wrong the moment two dialogs overlap: the second captures `hidden` as the value to put back, so closing it leaves the page locked with nothing open. A counter has no stale state — the property is set while anything holds the lock and removed when the last holder lets go.

decisions.decision: The modal motion band was wrong, and the tempo behind it was too slow
decisions.why: `motion.modal.duration` resolved to `motion.duration.slow`, which this system's own motion contract documents as “Continuous animation” — the spinner band. That was the category error; it is `medium-max` now, the slowest step of the entrance/exit band, which is where the expander's config names “(dialog, drawer)”. Fixing the band alone still left 545ms, because the medium band itself was too slow: Astryx's 175/410/975 tempo meant a menu took 410ms to appear. The seed came down to 130/210/700, so a dialog now enters in 280ms and a menu in 210ms. The bands kept their meanings and no role had to be remapped to one it does not belong to.

decisions.decision: The page's scroll is locked with the scrollbar's width held open
decisions.why: Hiding the overflow takes the scrollbar away and the page reflows into the space it occupied, so everything shifts sideways as the dialog opens and jumps back as it closes — more noticeable than the scrolling being prevented. The width is measured at lock time rather than tokenised, because it is whatever the browser and the reader's settings make it, and it is zero for overlay scrollbars.

decisions.decision: A native close is reported rather than ignored
decisions.why: `<form method="dialog">` is the documented HTML way to close a dialog, and the platform can close one for its own reasons too. Neither goes through `onClose`, and the effect that drives the dialog is keyed on `open`, so it never re-runs to notice — `open` went on claiming the dialog was showing, and the scroll lock stayed on the body with nothing open, leaving the page unable to scroll at all. The native `close` event now reports `external`, and only while React still believes the dialog is open, so the component's own `close()` is not mistaken for someone else's.

base.summary: A modal surface that takes over the screen.

tokens.enter transition: motion.modal.duration with motion.easing.enter, fading and rising
tokens.exit pointer-events: none while closing — the top layer is held for the exit, so the backdrop would go on catching clicks after the reader closed it

backdrop.summary: The wash over the inert page behind it. Its own token, added for this component: nothing else in the system dims the page, and a non-modal overlay must not. It transitions `overlay` alongside the dialog, which is what keeps the scrim on screen for the length of the exit rather than dropping it the instant the dialog starts closing.

size.summary: Three widths, derived from the control scale rather than stated: a dialog is measured in controls, and inventing a size.dialog.* family for three numbers would be a scale with one consumer. Flagged as a known gap if a fourth width ever appears.

tokens.sm max-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied by 10, or the viewport less its inset — whichever is smaller
tokens.md max-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied by 14, or the viewport less its inset — whichever is smaller
tokens.lg max-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied by 20, or the viewport less its inset — whichever is smaller

footer.summary: The actions, reading after the body they act on.

dismiss.summary: The close control. Same construction as Notice's: currentColor on a transparent background, so it cannot clash with the surface it sits on.

tokens.color: currentColor — inherited from the dialog's own foreground
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible
tokens.block alignment: centred on the title's first line, from type.heading.size and type.heading.line-height

example:
<Dialog
        open={open}
        onClose={() => setOpen(false)}
        title={title}
        description={description}
        size={size}
        dismissible={dismissible}
        initialFocus={cancelRef}
        footer={
          <>
            <Button ref={cancelRef} variant="secondary" onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>
              Cancel
            </Button>
            <Button variant={destructive ? "destructive" : "primary"} onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>
              {destructive ? "Delete" : "Save"}
            </Button>
          </>
        }
      >
        This cannot be undone.
      </Dialog>

name: icon
title: Icon
description: A Lucide glyph sized from the size.icon.* scale, inheriting its colour from the text around it.

props.name: icon
props.description: The Lucide component to render, passed as a value so the set stays tree-shakeable.
props.summary: The Lucide component to render, passed as a value rather than a name.
use: Any icon imported from `@rata/icons` — the curated set — or from `lucide-react` directly when the set is missing one.
Passing the component itself (`icon={Trash2}`), which is what keeps the icon set tree-shakeable: a string name would force every icon into the bundle.
dont: Rendering the Lucide component directly instead of through `Icon`. It would take Lucide's default 24px rather than a step from the scale, and it would not get the a11y switch below.
An emoji or a text glyph as a stand-in. Those inherit font metrics rather than the icon scale, so they will not line up with real icons beside them.
props.a11y: Rendered `aria-hidden` unless `label` is set — see `label`.

props.name: size
props.description: Which step of the `size.icon.*` scale to draw at. Defaults to following the surrounding text.
props.summary: Which step of the `size.icon.*` scale the glyph is drawn at. Defaults to following the surrounding text.
use: Leave it alone for anything with text near it — the default `text` step is 1.15em, so the glyph tracks whatever font-size it lands in and needs no decision per control.
`xs` / `sm` / `md` / `lg` only for a standalone glyph with no text to inherit from: a status dot in a table cell, or an icon-only control whose name is an `aria-label` rather than visible text.
`lg` when the glyph should render unscaled — 24px is Lucide's native artboard.
dont: Picking a fixed step to match a control's size. A control's `size` changes its box, not its text, so an icon inside it should not change either — and a fixed step stops matching the moment the surrounding text does change.
Mixing steps within one row of icons — they read as a set, so they measure as a set.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name, for an icon that carries meaning nothing else conveys.
props.summary: Accessible name, for an icon that carries meaning nothing else conveys.
use: An icon that is the only thing communicating something — a status glyph in a table cell with no adjacent text.
dont: An icon inside a `Button` with `iconOnly`. That button already carries the `aria-label` the contract requires, so labelling the icon too announces the same thing twice.
An icon sitting beside a visible text label. The text is the name; the icon is decoration and must stay hidden from assistive technology.
props.a11y: Present, the glyph becomes `role="img"` with this as its name. Absent, it is `aria-hidden` — the same switch `Spinner` uses for the same reason, and the reason the decorative case needs no thought to get right.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the glyph, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: A layout concern the parent cannot express, such as a margin token when the icon is not already inside a flex row with a gap.
dont: Overriding the size. The four steps are the scale; a fifth size written in a component's CSS is the drift `size.icon.*` exists to prevent — add a step to the scale instead.
Setting a colour. The glyph strokes with `currentColor` so it always matches the text it sits in; colouring it separately is how an icon ends up contradicting its own label.

usage.when: The most common pairing, and the one where the a11y split matters most.
usage.example:
<Button iconOnly aria-label="Delete row">
  <Icon icon={Trash2} />
</Button>
usage.notes: No `label` on the icon: the button owns the accessible name, so the glyph stays `aria-hidden`. `size` is left at `md`, which is what a 32px control wants.

usage.when: An action whose icon reinforces a word rather than replacing it.
usage.example:
<Button>
  <Icon icon={Download} />
  Export CSV
</Button>
usage.notes: No `size`: the default `text` step is 1.15em, so the glyph is sized from the button's own label and stays matched to it. The icon is decorative here, so it takes no `label` either.

usage.when: A status glyph in a dense row, with no adjacent text to name it.
usage.example: <Icon icon={CircleAlert} size="xs" label="Needs review" />
usage.notes: This is the only case that takes a `label`. Without one the row would announce nothing at all where a sighted user sees a warning.

base.summary: A glyph sized from the text around it, taking its colour from that text too.

tokens.width: size.icon.text — 1.15em, so it follows the inherited font-size. size.icon.xs / .sm / .md / .lg for a standalone glyph.
tokens.height: same step as width; the scale is one number and the glyph is square
tokens.stroke: currentColor — the icon inherits the colour of the text it sits in, so it needs no colour token of its own and cannot contradict its label
tokens.flex-shrink: 0 — a glyph beside text must not be squeezed by it, which is a layout fact rather than a token

name: menu
title: Menu
description: A transient list of actions anchored to a trigger.

props.name: trigger
props.summary: The control that opens the menu.
use: A `Button`. It is cloned to receive the trigger ARIA, a ref and the handlers.
dont: A `div` or a span. The trigger must be a real button or it is not reachable by keyboard, and none of the ARIA below means anything on a non-interactive element.
Passing `onClick` on it and expecting to be called. The menu owns that handler; put your own work in `onOpenChange`.
props.a11y: Receives `aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`. Its own text names the menu, which is why `label` is only for a trigger that has none.

props.name: children
props.description: `MenuItem` and `MenuSeparator` children, in the order they are read.
props.summary: `MenuItem` and `MenuSeparator`, in the order they are read.
use: Two to about seven actions. Longer than that and the reader is scanning, not choosing.
dont: Anything focusable that is not a `MenuItem`. The arrow keys walk the rows the menu knows about, and a stray button would be a tab stop the pattern does not account for.
A form. A menu is a list of actions; something to fill in belongs in a dialog.
props.a11y: Each row registers itself, so navigation follows DOM order rather than mount order — which is what the reader sees.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the menu is showing. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the menu is showing. Makes the component controlled.
use: Opening the menu from somewhere else, or keeping it open across a re-render you drive.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultOpen`. One of them owns the state.

Opening more than one at a time. The list is a `popover="auto"`, and the platform allows exactly one of those open at once — showing a second closes the first, and the menu reports that through `onOpenChange` rather than silently disagreeing with your state.
props.a11y: Controlled means the menu will not open unless you change this — the trigger still reports the request through `onOpenChange`, and `aria-expanded` follows whatever you set.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled menu. Conflicts with `open`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled menu.
use: Almost never. A menu that is open before the reader asked for it covers the thing they were looking at.
dont: Using it as a way to show the menu on load. That is what a `Notice` or an inline panel is for.
props.a11y: Focus is NOT moved into the menu, and that is deliberate: focus follows the reader's own action, and taking it on page load would be hostile. The first row is still the tab stop, so Tab reaches it and the arrow keys work from there. The same is true of setting `open` programmatically.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.summary: Called when the menu should open or close.
use: Controlled mode, to set `open`.
Uncontrolled mode, to react — closing a toolbar, or logging.
dont: Doing work that belongs in a row's `onSelect`. This fires for every close, including Escape and clicking away.

props.name: label
props.description: Names the list itself, for a trigger whose own name describes the button.
props.summary: Names the list itself, for a trigger whose own name describes the button.
use: An icon-only trigger, where the button is named "Row actions" and the list needs naming separately.
dont: A trigger with visible text. The text already names the menu, and a second name would win over the one the reader can see.
props.a11y: Becomes the menu's `aria-label` and suppresses the `aria-labelledby` pointing at the trigger — never both, because two names on one node is a 4.1.2 problem rather than a fallback.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the list, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Constraining the width when the actions are unusually long.
dont: Positioning it. Placement comes from anchor positioning in `menu.css`; a competing `position` here is how a menu ends up in the wrong place on one page only.

usage.when: The commonest case: a handful of things you can do to one item.
usage.example:
<Menu trigger={<Button variant="secondary">Actions</Button>}>
  <MenuItem onSelect={duplicate}>Duplicate</MenuItem>
  <MenuItem onSelect={download}>Download</MenuItem>
  <MenuSeparator />
  <MenuItem destructive onSelect={remove}>Delete</MenuItem>
</Menu>
usage.notes: The separator groups the destructive action away from the safe ones, so it is harder to hit by accident. `destructive` colours it; the separator is what actually puts distance between them.

usage.case: An icon-only trigger, which needs the list named separately
usage.when: A dense table where a labelled button would not fit.
usage.example:
<Menu
  label="Row actions"
  trigger={<Button iconOnly aria-label="Row actions" variant="tertiary"><Icon icon={Ellipsis} /></Button>}
>
  <MenuItem onSelect={edit}>Edit</MenuItem>
  <MenuItem destructive onSelect={remove}>Delete</MenuItem>
</Menu>
usage.notes: Both names are needed and they are not redundant: the button's `aria-label` names the control you press, and `label` names the list that appears. Without the second, the menu is announced with the button's name, which describes the wrong thing.

usage.case: Don't: a menu standing in for a choice that should be a form control
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.example:
{/* Don't: this is a select wearing a menu's clothes. */}
<Menu trigger={<Button>Sort: {sort}</Button>}>
  <MenuItem selected={sort === "name"} onSelect={() => setSort("name")}>Name</MenuItem>
  <MenuItem selected={sort === "date"} onSelect={() => setSort("date")}>Date</MenuItem>
</Menu>
usage.notes: Don't. A menu is a list of actions; a choice with a current answer is a `RadioGroup`, or a select once this system has one. `selected` exists for the narrow case where a menu genuinely reflects state — a view switcher — not as licence to build a picker out of actions.

behavior.summary: A trigger and a list in the top layer. The list carries the `popover` attribute, so it escapes every overflow and stacking context without a portal and gets light-dismiss from the platform; CSS anchor positioning places it against the trigger and flips it near a viewport edge. No measurement code and no dependency — which matters more here than usual, because this registry is a copy-paste channel and a dependency becomes an install step for every consumer.

decisions.decision: Focus always returns to the trigger on Escape and after a selection
decisions.why: It is what makes the menu usable by keyboard at all: close it and the reader has to be somewhere, and the only place that makes sense is where they were. The primitive reports the close and the wrapper does the focusing, since moving focus is a DOM act. Light-dismiss is the exception — the reader clicked something else, and taking focus back would undo their own action.

decisions.decision: Selection closes the menu before `onSelect` runs
decisions.why: So focus is already back on the trigger by the time the handler does anything. A handler that navigates, or opens a dialog, would otherwise be fighting a menu that is still tearing down, and the dialog would steal focus from a control that is about to vanish.

decisions.decision: A disabled row is reachable and announced
decisions.why: The `aria-disabled` rule this whole system follows: arrow keys reach it, a screen reader reads it, and activation is refused. Most menus skip disabled rows entirely, which makes the list a different length depending on whether you are looking or listening.

decisions.decision: Tab closes the menu without trapping focus
decisions.why: Someone tabbing through a page expects to keep going. Trapping focus is what a dialog does, because a dialog is modal and a menu is not.

decisions.decision: Typeahead cycles on a single character rather than buffering a prefix
decisions.why: A buffer has to be cleared after a pause, which needs a timer, which needs state — and the primitive is a pure function with neither. Repeating a key walks the matching rows, which is what typeahead is actually used for. Typing `de` to reach Delete past Duplicate is the part that is missing, and it is documented rather than faked. It also ignores a keypress with Ctrl, Meta or Alt held: `event.key` for Ctrl+D is just "d", so without that check a browser shortcut was indistinguishable from someone typing, and typeahead both hijacked the key and preventDefault'd it.

decisions.decision: The list's open state is driven imperatively, not by popovertarget
decisions.why: `popovertarget` would let the platform toggle the popover without telling React, and `open` would drift out of step with what is painted. The trigger's click goes through the primitive instead, and the popover's own `toggle` event is what keeps state honest when the platform closes it.

decisions.decision: The anchor name is generated per instance, not written in the stylesheet
decisions.why: `anchor-name` is a global ident, and the spec resolves a duplicated one to the LAST acceptable anchor in tree order. A single name in the CSS therefore made every menu on a page position itself against whichever trigger came last, which is invisible until a second menu exists. CSS cannot mint a unique ident, so the component passes one in as a custom property — on both the trigger and the list, because a sibling inherits nothing. It is sanitised: React 18's `useId` produces `:r0:` and a colon is not valid in an ident.

base.summary: A transient list of actions anchored to a trigger.

tokens.min-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied — the list should not be narrower than a control

separator.summary: A rule between groups of actions.

            label="Account"
            trigger={
              <Button iconOnly aria-label="Account" variant="tertiary">
                <Icon icon={User} />
              </Button>
            }
          >
            <MenuItem icon={Settings} onSelect={() => {}}>Settings</MenuItem>
            <MenuItem onSelect={() => {}}>Sign out</MenuItem>
          </Menu>

decisions.decision: Context, not cloneElement

decisions.decision: `value` defaults to the children when they are a plain string

decisions.decision: A checkable row is a different role, not a menuitem with an extra attribute

base.summary: One action. Its own focus ring, because the roving tabindex means an item — not the menu — is what focus lands on.

destructive.summary: An action that removes something. Uses the danger role's foreground on the menu's own surface — a pairing the token contracts verify for text at any size — rather than a tinted row, which would read as a status.

decisions.decision: It does not decide when it applies

decisions.decision: `value` is required and is the item's whole identity

base.summary: One option in a radio group. Circular, so its shape says 'one of these' before the label is read.

props.name: onValueChange

props.summary: Accessible name for the clear control.

usage.case: Filtering a list as you type

/>

usage.case: A committed query that went to the network
usage.when: The search costs something, so the reader needs to know it is happening.
usage.example:
<> {/* The count is what the reader needs, and Search cannot know it. */}

{pending ? "" : `${results.length} found`}

usage.case: Don't: a placeholder standing in for the label
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.

{/* Don't: the name disappears on the first keystroke. */}
<Search label="" placeholder="Search" />
usage.notes: Don't. A placeholder is not a name: it is gone as soon as someone types, several screen readers never read it, and `role="searchbox"` with no name is a 4.1.2 failure. `label` is required precisely so this cannot be written by accident — the empty string above is the only way to get close, and it is still wrong.

behavior.summary: A native `input[type="search"]`, which the platform maps to `role="searchbox"`. Its own construction rather than a `text-field` variant: a search has no validation states, is conventionally unlabelled on screen, carries a clear control, and answers Escape — none of which a text field does, and a `type` prop on TextField would have brought all four along as dead weight.

decisions.decision: Not a variant of TextField
decisions.why: They share a look and nothing else. A text field is a value being collected — it validates, it carries helper text, it is labelled on screen. A search is a question being asked: it has no invalid state, its label is normally hidden, and its Escape and clear behaviours exist nowhere else. Sharing the CSS is the right amount of sharing.

decisions.decision: Escape clears the field only when there is something to clear
decisions.why: Clearing on Escape is the convention, and implementing it unconditionally breaks every overlay a search sits inside: the field would swallow the key and a Dialog or Menu would stop closing. Empty, the key is left alone and bubbles to whatever should handle it. This is the whole reason the behaviour is in a primitive rather than an onKeyDown at the call site.

decisions.decision: The clear control is absent rather than disabled when the field is empty
decisions.why: There is nothing to clear, so there is nothing to announce or tab to. A disabled-but-present button would be a permanent stop in the tab order of every empty search box in the product.

decisions.decision: The platform's own clear button is suppressed

decisions.decision: Suggestions are deliberately out of scope
decisions.why: A search field that proposes completions is a combobox — `aria-expanded`, a popup listbox, `aria-activedescendant` and its own focus model. That is a different ARIA pattern, not a prop on this one, and building it in here would make the plain case carry machinery it never uses. base.summary: The field itself, matching text-field step for step so the two line up in a row — including its focus treatment, which is that component's documented departure from the system ring.

tokens.focus: outline theme.fg.primary at focus.ring-width, offset space.0, border darkened to match

size.summary: Height and inline padding only, matching button and text-field step for step.

clear.summary: The trailing clear control, present only when there is a query. Same construction as Notice's and Dialog's dismiss: currentColor on a transparent background.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

title: SideNav
description: A vertical navigation rail, grouped into named sections.

props.description: The destinations, grouped. One unlabelled section is a flat nav.
props.summary: The destinations, grouped. One unlabelled section is a flat nav.
use: A named section per group of related pages: "Billing", "Settings".
A single section with no `label` when there is nothing to group.
`items` on an entry for pages nested under it — it becomes a disclosure button rather than a link, and opens by default when one of its children is current.
`onClick` on an entry to intercept the navigation for a client-side router — the `href` stays real, so the row is still a link.
dont: A section per item. A group of one is a heading over nothing, and it reads as a mistake.

The current item carries `aria-current="page"` — the only non-colour cue it has, since the visual distinction is a background tint and a text tone. An entry with `items` becomes a disclosure button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, and its parent-of-the-current-page state is `aria-current="true"` rather than `"page"`, because you are not on it. The nested list is unmounted while collapsed rather than hidden, so nothing in it can be reached by a find-in-page while the group claims to be shut.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.

dont: Leaving the default when a page also has a `TopNav`. Two navigation landmarks need distinct names, and that is the one place they matter most.

props.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the nav, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Giving the rail its width, or making it stick — both layout decisions the component deliberately leaves to the page.
dont: Changing the item treatment. The current-page marker is load-bearing, and a rail that marks it differently from the top nav reads as a different product.

usage.when: The commonest case: enough pages that they need grouping.
usage.example:

  label="Invoices"
  sections={[
    {
      label: "Billing",
      items: [
        { label: "Invoices", href: "/invoices", current: true },
        { label: "Credit notes", href: "/credit-notes" },
      ],
    },

      label: "Setup",

        { label: "Templates", href: "/templates" },

usage.case: A flat rail, with nothing to group
usage.when: Few enough destinations that a heading over them would be noise.
usage.example:
<SideNav
  label="Settings"
  sections={[
    {
      items: [
        { label: "Profile", href: "/profile", current: true },
        { label: "Notifications", href: "/notifications" },
        { label: "Security", href: "/security" },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>

usage.case: A group with pages nested under it
usage.when: A destination that is itself a section of several pages.
usage.example:
<SideNav
  label="Invoices"
  sections={[
    {
      items: [
        { label: "All invoices", href: "/invoices" },
        {
          label: "Reports",
          items: [
            { label: "Revenue", href: "/reports/revenue", current: true },
            { label: "Ageing", href: "/reports/ageing" },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>

Note the two kinds of current again: the child is `aria-current="page"`, and its parent is `"true"` because you are only inside the area it leads to.

usage.case: Don't: a section for every item
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.notes: Don't. A group of one is a heading over nothing: it doubles the reading length, and a screen reader announces a list of one item under a name that repeats it. Those are two flat items in one unlabelled section.

behavior.summary: A `<nav>` containing one list per section. No primitive and no keyboard handling: every link is its own tab stop, which is what navigation should be. Unlike TopNav this claims no page-level landmark beyond the nav itself — where the rail sits, and whether it is inside a `<main>` or beside it, is the caller's layout decision.

decisions.decision: Sections are the only shape, even for a flat list
decisions.why: A side nav exists because there are enough destinations to group; a flat one is the special case, not the default. Offering both `items` and `sections` would mean two mutually exclusive props and a rule about which wins — so a flat nav is one unlabelled section, which costs a pair of braces and removes the ambiguity entirely.

decisions.decision: A section's label names its list rather than being a heading
decisions.why: Same reasoning as Notice's title: a nav cannot know what heading level it sits under, and a wrong one breaks heading navigation for the whole page. The label is a plain element with an id, and the list points at it with `aria-labelledby` — so the group is announced with its name and the document outline is untouched.

decisions.decision: Collapsing to an icon-only rail is out of scope
decisions.why: A collapsed rail hides the labels, which is the point of collapsing and also the problem: a sighted reader then needs the name on hover, and this system has no Tooltip. Shipping the collapse without one would trade an accessible nav for a row of unexplained glyphs. It belongs with a Tooltip, not before one.

decisions.decision: The current page is stated per item, as in TopNav
decisions.why: Only the caller knows whether /invoices/123 counts as being on /invoices. Matching a path here would have to guess between exact and prefix and would be silently wrong for someone either way. It is shown as a tinted row rather than an edge marker: the marker was removed on request, which leaves the visual cue entirely colour and `aria-current` as the only cue that is not.

decisions.decision: A nested group is a disclosure expanded in place, not a popover
decisions.why: An item with `items` becomes a button that expands a list beneath it. Not a menu, for the reason getDisclosureProps documents: `role="menu"` announces a keyboard model a list of links does not have. And not a popover either, unlike TopNav's — a rail scrolls vertically, so a nested list pushes what follows it down and nothing has to escape an overflow. Keeping it inline also keeps the nesting visible, which is most of what a rail is for.

decisions.decision: A group holding the current page starts open
decisions.why: Not a convenience: a reader whose page sits inside a collapsed group cannot see where they are, which is the one question a nav exists to answer. `defaultExpanded` overrides it for the rare case where a group is long enough that opening it costs more than it explains.

decisions.decision: Rows carry an optional onClick, and still require a real href
decisions.why: Found by trying to build the playground's own rail out of this component: the rows navigate client-side, and with no way to intercept the click there was no way to use it without a full page load. The href stays required rather than becoming optional, because it is what makes the row a link — middle-click, copy-address and crawlers all depend on it, and a nav built from handlers with no addresses behind them loses all three without appearing to.

base.summary: The rail. No background of its own: it sits on whatever surface the page gives it, so the same component works against the canvas and inside a panel. Its width is the page's to set.

section.summary: A named group. The label is the list's accessible name, not a heading — a nav cannot know what heading level it sits under.

item.summary: One destination, filling the rail's width so the whole row is the target.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

item-current.summary: The page you are on: a tinted row, plus aria-current in the markup. The tint is the role's subtle step with fg.primary on it — a pairing the token contracts verify for text at any size — not the saturated fill, which is a non-text indicator tone.
